newsitem.title: CHINA: China issues directive to unify worker pensions.
newsitem.headline: China issues directive to unify worker pensions.

text.p: China has issued a directive on unifying its disjointed pension system in hopes that reform will give a boost to ailing state firms and keep workers happy, officials and state media said on Wednesday.

The State Council, or cabinet, had recently issued the Decision on Establishing a Unified Enterprise Worker Pension System, a policy that would set a national standard for pensions after two years of pilot projects, a council official said.
"This is a major milestone in the reform of China's social insurance system," said an editorial in the Communist Party mouthpiece, the People's Daily.

Senior officials hailed the directive as a major step in the reform of state enterprises, which are saddled with having to care for rising numbers of retired and redundant workers amid soaring losses.

"A major aspect of pension reform is to lessen the burden on enterprises and to support and serve enterprise reform," the China Securities newspaper quoted Li Tieying, minister of the State Commission for Restructuring the Economy, as saying.
"The Decision... will lessen the burden of social tasks of enterprises, strengthening their competitive ability and vigour for development," it quoted Li as saying.
The new policy would help to create a pensions system that would ensure a minimum standard of living for retired workers, something that some current welfare programmes were unable to do, Li said.
Beijing views the prospect of hordes of unemployed workers with no income or welfare benefits as a serious threat to stability and hopes to reform state firms without sparking social unrest.

China has been moving slowly to replace its pay-as-you-go retirement scheme -- which pools contributions -- with a system of personal accounts that would enable workers to take benefits as they move from one job to another.

Li gave no details of what the unified plan will look like, but authorities have been moving towards a system that would have employees contribute about eight percent of their wages to be matched by three percent from the employer.
Li did not say who would manage the funds or how they would be invested.
The directive would help to solve problems posed by having to merge a myriad of local systems and in protecting funds from abuse, Li said.
"The misuse of pension money is a relatively serious problem," Li said. "They must be used entirely to support elderly workers."
In 1996, workers and enterprises put 117.0 billion yuan ($14.1 billion) into pension funds, which had paid out 103.0 billion yuan, the State Council official said.
